title: One, two, three
hookLine: the Tao produced one, one two, two three, three all things; all carry yin and embrace yang (Tao Te Ching 42)

lines: YIN AND YANG, IN THEIR SETTING.
cards: One, two, three. It's how a child counts before jumping into a pool, how a band counts in a song, how a race begins.
Chapter forty-two of the Tao Te Ching counts too, and in a handful of words it gets from the way to everything there is.
Right after the counting, it names two words that have traveled far beyond the book, onto t-shirts and tattoos and necklaces split in half: yin and yang. Here they are, where this chapter puts them.

teach.b: First, the count. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things." It reads like a family tree, or a seed becoming a forest.

teach.h: THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY WHAT THEY ARE.
teach.b: The chapter never says what one, two and three are. Some readers take one as the first unity, two as yin and yang, and three as what happens when the two blend. Others leave the numbers as a rhythm: from one, many.
The text stays quiet, and it's fine to let it. Third, the two words.

teach.h: ALL THINGS CARRY YIN, EMBRACE YANG.
teach.b: All things, the chapter says, carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and a blending breath brings them into harmony.
Legge doesn't even write yin and yang; he renders them as the Obscurity and the Brightness. Either way, the picture isn't a fight between good and bad.
Every single thing carries both at once, and the harmony comes from the blend, not from one side winning. Fourth, in a single day.

It's easy to sort a day into opposites and want only one side: rest and not work, praise and not criticism, sunshine and not shade. The chapter's picture is gentler. Effort and ease in the same breath.
Strength and tenderness in the same person. A sad morning and a good afternoon in the same day. The work isn't to get rid of one.
It's to let the two find their balance.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-two's yin and yang as a picture of opposites held together in balance, and some use it as a reminder not to cling to one side of a pair.

o: the two that every thing carries, blended into harmony
a pair of rival gods who divided up the world
the forces of good and evil, locked in a war

p: carried by all things at once

s: chapter forty-two explains exactly what one, two and three are
the text never says. readers fill the gap in different ways.
in the chapter, yin and yang are good and evil at war
every thing carries both, and harmony comes from the blend.
Legge renders yin and yang as the Obscurity and the Brightness
he translates the words instead of keeping the Chinese.

games.q: a day hands you a hard task and good news at the same time. what does chapter forty-two's picture suggest?
o: focus only on the good news.
carry both, and let them balance.
push the hard task away until tomorrow.
games.why: the chapter says all things carry yin and embrace yang together. the harmony comes from the blend, not from one side winning.

practice: Breathe in, then out: neither one is the good one, and you need both. Look around for light and shadow side by side, then check your body for somewhere tense and somewhere soft.
Don't fix either; just notice that both are there at once, and let the breath move between them.

wordCard.voice: Yin yang. In chapter forty-two, the two that every single thing carries at once, brought into harmony by a blending breath. Today's word.
